Mr. Speaker, yesterday we were debating motions put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), motions Nos. 5, 6 and 11. These are proposed amendments to Clause 4 of the Canada Shipping Act.
Hon. Members must realize that Clause 4 of the Bill will provide the Government with the authority to recover the cost of providing Coast Guard services. This is certainly a departure from the prior practice. In the past, these services were not charged for. There was no user fee for Coast Guard services. In Clause 4 the Government proposes to impose such charges. Indeed, under the legislation the Minister will have the authority to set the fee, not only for Coast Guard services, but fees for ice-breaking, navigational aids, dredging services, soundings and search and rescue. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, can you imagine what such a move will do to the East Coast, not only to fishermen but to farmers? Can Your Honour imagine what it will do to the economy of the East Coast of Canada? Do Members opposite from Atlantic Canada not realize the drastic affect this measure will have on the livelihoods of their constituents, since all these charges will have to be passed on down the line to the consumer?

I was saying: Where are the back-bench Conservative Members from Atlantic Canada? Clause 4 will have very drastic effects on fishermen, farmers and consumers in Atlantic Canada. Surely those back-bench Members from Atlantic Canada know that the area suffers from one of the highest unemployment rates in the country. We know that economically the area does not enjoy the same level of activity as does central Canada and some parts of western Canada. I am aggrieved that Conservative back-benchers who talk big when they are in their ridings about how they will fight the Government and how they will be tough on issues are just tabby cats when they come here to the House of Commons. They just sit in their places and say absolutely nothing when measures such as those envisioned in Clause 4 are put on the record.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to these motions in order to ask for common sense in the deliberation of Bills that are supposed to be in the best interests of all the citizens of Canada, and, in particular, in this case, the citizens who live in the Province of Quebec where the Great St. Lawerence Seaway is found. That Seaway is a very vital link to the lives and the economy of our province. I think it would be irresponsible, to say the least, and even unfair to increase the costs to fishermen in this way.
As we all know, the fishing industry is a depressed industry at this time. Fishermen have asked for a degree of relief. There have been some serious problems in that industry. I would suggest that we are making a very reasonable request. We are asking for a delay. Rather than simply opposing for the sake of
opposing, we are recommending a delay so that we can study from an intelligent perspective the potential negative impact of Clause 4 of Bill C-75.
I think that the Minister would be most disconcerted if we were to allow this Bill to go ahead. I think we are saving him a great deal of heartache. The Minister of Employment and Immigration would have been quite thrilled if we had asked for a delay until the report of the Forget Commission came in. If we had, she would not have found herself so embarrassed today with respect to the reaction to unemployment insurance benefits and severance pay.
In a sense, Clause 4 gives the Minister the authority to charge but does not tell people what they are being charged for. It gives the Minister the authority to determine what he is going to do with the lives of people without letting those people know what he is going to do with their lives. How will that impact on the quality of their lives? I would like to recommend that we take cognizance of the growing discomfort of many groups in society and give heed to what they have to say.
The Government prides itself on having developed a very good rapport with our good neighbour to the South and has been negotiating for an open ear and an open mind. If this is to be the case, I would strongly recommend that the Government listen to our American friends and neighbours and that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) take heed of a letter he received on April 14 so that American-Canadian relations may improve all along the way. The Seaway does not belong only to Canada; it is a shared waterway. What we do here has an impact upon the American side of the border.
I should like to refer to a letter signed by a number of American Senators and dated April 14, 1986. It was directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister from the Executive Director of the Great Lakes Commission. It reads:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
The Great Lakes Commission is deeply concerned about proposed Bill C-75, which would authorize the imposition of cost recovery for Canadian Coast Guard services.
The Commission respects Canada's need to raise additional revenues. The Commission also accepts Canada's choice of user fees as one vehicle to accomplish that end. However, the Commission, as the only co-ordinating and advocacy agency established by the States and approved by Congress to provide a collective voice for the eight Great Lakes states on water resource and related issues, would be remiss if it did not express opposition to the current language of Bill C-75.
The Commission has monitored the progress of C-75 in Parliament and participated in regional discussions about potential impacts of the Coast Guard cost recovery provision, Clause 4. Commission testimony was presented to the legislative committee in Ottawa on February 13,1986.
It is too bad it was not listened to. The letter continues:
The Commission emphasized four points believed to be necessary before navigation cost recovery legislation can be successfully implemented:
This is one of the reasons we are asking for the delay. It continues:
May 1, 1986

1.	Federal user fees should be uniform in application from seaport to seaport and from coastal range to coastal range. (Uniformity maintains the current competitive relationship among ports.)
2.	There must be a clear determination of the purposes for which fees are to be collected and the activities to which they are to be applied. (This is critical to the ultimate acceptability of any system adopted.)
If they do not know what it is for, why apply it? The letter continues:
3.	Any fee system, as it may affect the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence system, should be co-ordinated with United States' cost recovery programs and should give due consideration to total elimination of existing St. Lawrence Seaway system tolls.
4.	Any user fee proposal should involve thorough public consultations with all user groups which should take place before initial application of fees and before any subsequent changes in levels of fees.
Ambassador Gotlieb's presence at the Commission's semi-annual meeting in Washington, D.C. March 12 was sincerely appreciated. In his remarks about Bill C-75 to the Commission, the Ambassador stated: "There is no doubt that your interests as a vitally affected party will not be ignored in the development of any user fee program.'' These are positive words, but Final language from the legislative committee virtually mandates a segment charge (unequal between ports and port ranges) which could be devastating to Canadian and U.S. Great Lakes maritime and water transport dependent industries, leading to loss of maritime, industrial and agricultural jobs.
The Great Lakes Commission's views with respect to Clause 4 in Bill C-75 are supported by the Great Lakes Congressional delegation and regional maritime interests. A March 25 letter to Transport Minister Mazankowski from several Great Lakes Congressmen and a March 7 letter from Great Lakes Senators to Ambassador Gotlieb are attached for your reference.
The Commission believes that binational co-ordination regarding the future of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence transportation system is imperative now, more than ever before. The Great Lakes Commission along with the Great Lakes Senators and Representatives, is ready and willing to work with Canadian federal, provincial and private sector interests to see that our unique and shared Great Lakes-St. Lawrence River resource is maintained and improved for the benefit of our two countries and the world.
Sincerely,
James Fish Executive Director
In light of the very serious implications of the Bill, in light of the loss of confidence we have already suffered in the St. Lawrence Seaway system as a result of unfortunate damage resulting in diminished traffic, and in light of the changes which are being suggested, I wonder what the Province of Quebec would have to say. As a last measure to plead for the delay we have proposed, I should like to read a letter which was directed to our Washington Ambassador, and I think our word should be honoured. It reads:
Dear Mr. Ambassador:
We wish to thank you for your recent letter concerning legislative action on Clause 4 of Bill C-75 currently pending before the Canadian Parliament. It was reassuring to us to learn that Bill C-75 was before a special legislative committee of Parliament for detailed analysis and that the Minister of Transport would be establishing a committee to consider the views of all affected parties prior to any decision to implement Coast Guard user fees.
The Executive Director of the Great Lakes Commission, Mr. James Fish, has informed us of his testimony on this issue before the legislative committee on February 13, 1986. We commend the Canadian Government for sponsoring hearings on this important legislation and view such hearings as a most constructive process. However, we, along with Mr. Fish, remain concerned about

the potential damage to Canadian and U.S. shipping and related activities stemming from imposition of a Coast Guard user fee in addition to the current seaway tolls.
These tolls have already been increased. It continues:
While the United States Government is currently considering user fee legislation for navigation projects, proposed parallel provisions in this legislation would provide for a rebate of or credit toward seaway tolls paid by shippers to the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation. Such complementary provisions are important in preserving and preferably increasing the use of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway navigation system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a moment or two to talk about the whole concept of user fees, particularly as they apply to the Coast Guard. I do so with the. benefit of some knowledge of matters such as this. I do a bit of sailing and I have a certain amount of knowledge-I do not pretend to be an expert by any means-of what happens, the way people view the Coast Guard, and the way in which it is used out of necessity by small craft owners.
Let us take a look at the Coast Guard and what it is. Basically it performs two functions. One function is the policing of boundaries, which it does in an exemplary way. The other function is a safety one. It performs a safety function for people who require assistance from time to time when they are on the water. I want to address myself to that aspect for a few moments.
I should like to draw an analogy between persons travelling by automobile down a highway who have problems with their automobiles. They are able to call for the Ontario Provincial Police, the RCMP, or the local constabulary and obtain assistance. There is no charge. The assistance is offered and given; whatever is required to be done is done. That person is able to go on his way and continue to operate as he anticipated he would. The same basic service must be available on the water, and the same principle must prevail. A person, whether or not he can afford to dig into his pocket and pay, must be able to call for and get help from the Coast Guard if that person deems it necessary in the circumstances.
The difficulty in the user fee concept, and this is where we have a problem, is that no one knows at this point whether it is the intention of the Government to establish a user fee for such an event. What you will have happening, I think, having watched boaters for a number of years, is that people will be reluctant to call for the assistance they need when they need it if there is a fee attached to getting that assistance.
Let me give an example. You are in a narrows where the water is a little rough but it is protected reasonably well from wind. You have trouble with the motor of your boat. You can get it going but it won't keep going. At this point what you do is radio ship to shore and seek the assistance of the Coast Guard. The Coast Guard comes out and will do one of a
number of things. They will either give you assistance in the form of gasoline if that is your problem, they may arrange to have you towed to a safe harbour or they may arrange to simply watch over you while you do the work to make sure that nothing untoward occurs, either by virtue of you being in a shipping lane and unable to get out of it or perhaps by virtue of the tide itself taking you into danger.
I have seen many boaters who have temporary problems with motors of their boats. I have seen them on many occasions call for assistance, but between the time they make the call and the assistance arrives they are able to correct the problem. They wait to notify the Coast Guard when they arrive, but then the boaters move on under their own power. If the person out on the boat knows there is going to be a charge levied against him for asking for that service, there will be a delay, I predict, in requesting the assistance needed. Boaters will spend more time monkeying around trying to solve the problem before making the call. As a result, rather than a safer system on the water, we will have a less safe system on the water. I suggest that it does not take a genius to see this.
I invite any Member of the House of Commons to spend a few days this coming summer on the St. Lawrence River, which is close by, or even on the Ottawa River, and I don't personally boat there-it doesn't happen on the Ottawa River as it turns out-and see the numbers of times on the St. Lawrence River that the Coast Guard is requested to provide assistance. If people are reluctant to seek that assistance by virtue of the cost attendant upon getting it, potential dangers will result. For the tiny financial benefit to the coffers of the Government of Canada by virtue of the imposition of a user fee in situations such as that, the risks of delays will far outweigh them.
I am pleading, I suppose, for some understanding of human nature. That is all. If your car is coughing and sputtering on the highway, all you need to do is pull over, walk and get assistance. You can if you wish, if you have the means, get assistance from local police forces. On the water, however, it is an entirely different and much more difficult situation. There should be no impediment put in the way of a person on the water being able to call for and get assistance. I suggest small though the user fee may be, it will become an impediment and, therefore, will in itself create a more hazardous situation than previously existed, and I consider that to be folly on the part of Government.
I can well appreciate the Government's concern over finances. I can well understand that the Government wants to find ways to levy the cost out a little more equitably-I am not sure that is the right term in this circumstance-but in this particular instance safety is far more important than the minimal dollar return. Since we are encouraging people to utilize the waters surrounding Canada, and we are encouraging people to vacation and use those facilities in Canada, we should be prepared to provide the necessary policing force required to meet the potential dangers that will exist.
May 1, 1986

I listened yesterday to one of my colleagues who made a point, perhaps a little facetiously but nevertheless a valid one. The imposition of a user fee for Coast Guard use is a little bit like imposing the user fee for calling the police or the fire department. If you stop to think about it, it is ludicrous. It would be outrageous if we were to start now to impose user fees if you happen to need the assistance of the police. What if you made the call and they came, stood at your door and said: "We will give you a hand but there is a user fee". That would be ridiculous. I do not think anyone would contemplate it.
Mir. Rodriguez: What happens if you say you can't afford it?

As my colleague suggests, if you say you can't afford it, they won't give you help. I do not know whether that would be the case or not, but no one would ever contemplate such a stupid thing, not even Conservatives. Yet that is what is being suggested. We are suggesting that the police on the water can charge you for calling for their assistance while the police on the land in similar circumstances do not, and would never consider it.
I suggest that, if for no other reason than the reason I mentioned, this particular part of this Bill should be withdrawn. We should try to get some sanity into the debate and some understanding of the potential consequences. This is not a big item, this is not an item that requires a great deal of deliberation or something the Government requires to keep the coffers full. This will not make substantial difference to the over-all fiscal or financial affairs of the country, but it will make a difference in my judgment, and my judgment is based on experience of what the likely consequences will be with regard to safety on the waters of Canada that are currently under the jurisdiction of the Coast Guard. I ask that the Government withdraw this part of the Bill, show some common sense and recognize the potential hazard it is about to create.

Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill C-
75.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that although this is a subject that does not directly concern my riding, I have been listening to the debate in the House for some time, and I think a few comments are in order.
Bill C-75 bears the following title: "An Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Maritime Code Act and the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act in consequence thereof."
Mr. Speaker, upon reading this Bill, I think we cannot but agree, and support most if not all of the provisions of this legislation. When it is a matter of improving safety and protecting the environment, and when provision is made to update the Canada Shipping Act, and finally, the reference to
Canada Shipping Act
implementing a whole series of international conventions within a reasonable timeframe, I think it stands to reason that we should agree with the objectives and goals and in fact with everything provided under Bill C-75.
However, Mr. Speaker, there is Clause 4, and I think this is the basic and main reason why so many Members have reacted to this Bill. Whether or not we are affected by the consequences or impact of this Bill, I feel that after a careful look at the provisions of Clause 4, we have a duty to rise and protest most emphatically against a provision that I see as an insult to democracy, as a totally undemocratic gesture, as a weapon the Minister wants to keep in reserve in order to have absolute control over this very important sector. I think the amendments could have been approved so that this institution, so that we as Members of Parliament, in our democratic system, would be involved in a review or any future changes concerning the fee schedule.
When I decided to speak on this matter, Mr. Speaker, I tried to get hold of some testimony, some briefs that were presented when the Bill was considered in Committee, and in my humble opinion, the one I have here, that was presented by the Association des operateurs de navires du Saint-Laurent clearly and succinctly identifies the problem and the dramatic and extremely tragic consequences of the provisions of Clause 4. For instance, we can read the following on page 2 of the brief presented by the Association des operateurs de navires du Saint-Laurent on January 29, 1986: We reached the following conclusion. We agree with most of the provisions of this Bill- and that is exactly what my colleagues have been saying in the House-but there is one major objection concerning Clause 4: it should be the subject of legislation after due consultation with the interested parties, not before as is the case now.
Still at the bottom of page 2, they go on to say this: However, we think that Clause 4 should not have been smuggled in with the Bill, and such a radical change in the operations of the Coast Guard should not have been made without first discussing the matter with the interested parties. What stands out most in this exercise is the antidemocratic approach, so these people went to the trouble of raising a series of questions about Clause 4.
Just to show that my remarks are relevant, Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to mention some of the questions raised about Clause 4. For example, they ask: Which services will have to be paid for? Will it be navigational aids? Will it be environmental protection, dredging, de-icing, training schools, search and rescue operations, or all such services as a whole? On what criteria will operations be based? Will it be tonnage, the value of the goods, the size of the ship, the number of times a ship crosses imaginary lines in the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence River, or the Arctic gulf? When he was queried about this, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) said that his department planned to recover 15 per cent of the costs. Does that mean costs across Canada? In other words, will each area have to cover a specified percentage

May 1, 1986
Canada Shipping Act
of the expenditures incurred in regionalizing the Canadian Coast Guard?
Mr. Speaker, I could go on like this for a good ten minutes merely listing the issues raised by Clause 4. But in conclusion, I will give you a final instance in which it seems extremely complex and disquieting, even shocking to leave such an important matter to the discretion of the minister, with no way for this House, for us, Members of Parliament, to participate and defend the interests they are representing. The following example is given: Admittedly, a major part of winter expenses of the Canadian Coast Guard on the St. Lawrence River goes to environment protection-opening up the channel for the water to flow faster and without ice jams. Certainly, the movement of large container and other ships also makes a major contribution to de-icing the St. Lawrence River. The daily traffic of large ships contributes to and is in itself a deicing operation. Will they be refunded that part for which they contributed to that vital work, or will the Canadian Coast Guard benefit from the work that is in effect done by the large carriers?
All those questions remain unanswered, Mr. Speaker. All are concerns for those interested in transportation, all are also matters that are very disquieting for fishermen and a large part of our population, for these men and women living in Northern Canada, Northern Quebec, who depend on water transportation for food supplies. Clearly, if the charge is to be increased to the point where it becomes a major component, this will lead to substantial increases in the price of goods that are transported along the Seaway, and accordingly Canadian men and women in those areas will have to pay the greater part of the costs.
Another matter that seems important to me is that in the area of shipping, as in transportation in general, operators usually run on one-, two-, three-, or five-year contracts. Here is the situation. Once a company has obtained a two-, or three-year contract for shipping goods from one point to another, His Highness the minister suddenly decides from high above that he will increase the rates, after consulting a few officials who know nothing about the problem. Have you thought for a minute of the various consequences? In my view, this might very well disrupt an industry which is already very much affected and which does not need such confusion and complexity.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit it is really sad that a significant number of good aspects of Bill C-75 are spoiled by such provisions that are both unreasonable and unacceptable as far as elementary democracy is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively, as I always do, to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). He made some good points but he did not carry his analogies far enough. He said that a person involved in an automobile accident might expect the
police to provide certain emergency or safety services without charge. If you were in a car accident, the car was on fire and you were trapped inside, the police might be expected to extinguish the fire and extricate you from the vehicle. They might be expected to provide traffic directions around the scene of the accident. They do all all this at public expense and no expense to the person involved in the accident.
There are certain things that might be undertaken for which you would expect to pay. You would expect to pay, for example, the ambulance charges if you had to go to a hospital. You would not expect the police or some public body to pay for the towing charge of your car to be taken to the garage. You certainly would not expect any repairs on the car to be done at public expense.
We have the same types of concepts involved in what we are debating with respect to Coast Guard services here today. The Government obviously has no intention of levying a charge for those immediate emergency and safety services. What the Government might want to make a charge for is certain commercial types of services rendered by the Coast Guard. This is where the Opposition fails to make that distinction.
Charges for ice-breaking, towing, sounding, in many cases make eminent good sense. I have had occasion in the past to contract with a navigation company to go into areas that were not sounded. They have to sound the channel and they make an extra charge for that. The vessels have to slow down to get into that area and they have to take soundings as they go along. It makes sense that they should charge extra for that service. It would not make sense for me to be able to call up the Coast Guard and say, "Go and sound that channel", and the public is going to pay for it, as it is a commercial undertaking on my part. I am the one that is going to benefit from the shipping that takes place and nobody else. It would make eminent sense in that circumstance if the Coast Guard were to provide that service that I should have to pay for it.
The same can be said for certain ice-breaking services. If you accidently get stuck in an ice-pack, you want to be able to call the Coast Guard to come to break the ice and get you out of there. That is an emergency type of undertaking. If you know that you want to ship out a cargo of goods, or get some merchandise out of a location that is ice-bound and you know of this in advance you can either contract with a privately-owned ice-breaker to go in and escort your cargo-carrying vessel, or maybe you can get the Coast Guard to do it. If the Coast Guard does it, why should it be done at public expense? Of course it should not. It should be paid for by the person who reaps the commercial advantage. That is all that has been said in the provisions that have been presented here by the Government. In circumstances like that where it is a commercial-type service that has been rendered by the Coast Guard then there ought to be a schedule of fees. It ought not to be done at the expense of the taxpayer. The person who receives
May 1, 1986

the commercial advantages ought to pay a user fee for that service.
All the arguments that have been presented today by the Opposition when speaking of commercial-type services does not make sense. I will certainly vote against the proposed amendment.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by saying I listened with consternation and amazement to the comments by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). If there are any area, because of their geographic position and isolation, which get hit in the worst possible way by this concept of user-pay, they are those isolated areas like the Northwest Territories. Whether you look at transportation or anything else, the costs to the people who live there are much higher than everybody else. They would have to pay for the things that they get, which is what user-pay principle means I cannot understand how a Member who represents an area like that could take the very narrow,
Canada Shipping Act
"business is the only thing that counts", attitude he took. He seems to be living in an era of 50 years ago. If we applied the user-pay principle to the person who got sick and had to see a doctor, or a person who had to go to hospital, or a person who had to depend on his own ability to provide for a pension after she or he retires, those people would be in a terrible situation.
I want to say a few words about this Bill and the concept of user-pay for transportation and shipping in the St. Lawrence Seaway. I want to put on the record that the opposition to that principle is not just opposition by our political Party. Let me put on the record the views expressed by the Minister of Highways and Transportation for the Province of Saskatchewan. I am sure the Hon. Member from Western Arctic knows that they have a Conservative Government. He said the following:
Any increase in costs to users of the Great Lakes/St. Lawrence Seaway system will result in producers looking for transport services which are cheaper. As a result, some traffic may be diverted to the U.S. transportation system causing loss of Canadian jobs.
I have recently written to the Hon. Don Mazankowski-and advised him that the imposition of charges to defray the costs of the Coast Guard are ill advised-
We have the Western Regional Advisory Council, Alberta Economic Development, another Conservative province. They say the following:
The introduction of any regulation which will create an additional cost to the port and port users must not militate against the use of Canadian ports. We are most concerned that Clause 4 of the act which deals with cost recovery will impact negatively on Canada's international competitive position, by forcing business away.
Let me quote from the Minister of Highways and Transportation of my own province, who says the following:
If this clause in the Bill is allowed to remain, it will lead to efforts towards full cost recovery which is beyond the limited financial capabilities of grain producers and other shippers and consumers.
The continued pursuit of the "user pay" philosophy without regard for the ability of shippers and consumers to pay will inevitably cripple the flow of the nation's commerce.
The National Farmers' Union said:
In its preoccupation to trim the federal deficit, the Government is in effect telling farmers through this bill that the national interest can best be served by still further increasing farm costs at a time when farmers are in very serious financial straits.
We regard the St. Lawrence Seaway as a national asset that should be maintained in the national interest. It does not make good economic sense to raise rates in the face of declining demand.
There is no question an additional charge in any way placed on transportation at this time will in fact mean disaster to more producers. It will mean producers going broke.
I represent an urban constituency which has a very small number of farmers. However, I do represent many railway workers. There have been major lay-offs at CPR and CNR, the likes of which we have not seen since the 1930s. The prime reason for these lay-offs is that the shipment of grain has decreased dramatically.
Canadian wheat producers are facing very unfair competition from the United States and the European community,

May 1, 1986
Canada Shipping Act
both of which are subsidizing their grain farmers to a tremendous extent. These factors make it more difficult for farmers to sell their grain, which means that less grain will be shipped. As a result, the railway workers in my constituency will have a more difficult time holding their jobs with CNR and CPR, where there have already been too many lay-offs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), who consented to my intervention at this time. He recognizes that while this matter is of great importance to him, as a Member from Atlantic Canada it is indeed of greater importance to me.
That is why I am rather amazed that Members opposite, particularly Members from Atlantic Canada such as the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), support the thrust of this legislation which will cause additional costs. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) supports the Government in its attempt to add additional costs to fishermen for navigational aids, sounding, dredging, vessel traffic services, ice-breaking services and marine aid. I am very appalled that those Members would want to promote user fees for those types of services used by our primary producers.
It is likely that this legislation will be proclaimed by the Government of Canada and become the law with which people in my Province of Nova Scotia and other provinces will have to comply. It will be a great impediment to those who seek to make their living from the sea and by other means. For instance, this legislation will have a traumatic effect on the Prince Edward Island potato industry. That industry submitted a brief to the legislative committee that was studying Bill C-75 and the various amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. Given the recent events in Prince Edward Island, I would have thought that Members opposite who have a short time left to represent that province in the Parliament of Canada, would take heed of the message given by the people of Prince Edward Island to the provincial Conservative Party that they do not like this sort of action by the Government of Canada. User fees for these very important services will affect them in a very dramatic way.
The Prince Edward Island potato industry states in their brief that they are vigorously opposed to the introduction of charges relating to navigational services until an impact study on the potato industry's export business has been conducted. That industry knows that these user fees will have an extremely negative impact on their industry. Has the Government or have the Conservative Members of Parliament from Prince Edward Island provided that impact study? Have they provided the information that would address that issue? No. They support the Bill as it stands. One could conclude as a result of their lack of action and concern on behalf of the people whom they represent that they want to see that
particular industry decline even further than it has. I would hope that the message given to former Premier Lee of Prince Edward Island would be sufficient to make Members opposite cognizant that this legislation is discriminatory and unfair to the primary producers in Canada so much so that they would stand in their places and reject this legislation.
Not only do potato farmers find this legislation destructive to their industry, that sentiment is shared by the primary producers in the fishing industry. I am talking about those individuals who must rise early in the morning, set out to catch the fish and return to have their catch processed. There seems to be a myth that these primary producers are making large sums of money. However, we are not talking about National Sea, we are referring to that small independent fisherman who must go out on his boat on a daily basis to try to make sufficient money to earn a livelihood for his family. The Government is telling those fishermen that they may continue to do that, but they will not only pay personal income taxes, there will now be a charge for dredging services and navigational services. If that is not enough, the Government will charge for ice-breaking services and any marine aid that may be necessary.
The Government has singled out those small individual primary producers in our country and introduced discriminatory legislation that will affect them in a very negative way. That is very unlike what the Government has done for other sectors of the economy. I suggest that Members of Parliament from Atlantic Canada visit the wharfs and bays of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick to explain to the people there how the Government can provide $500,000 in capital gains tax provisions, provide millions of dollars in bail-outs to banks in western Canada, or provide special unrestricted income to the oil and gas industry in this country, yet the small independent primary producers in this country must pay more. Where is the fairness? Where is the equality of opportunity?
Unfortunately, the Prince Edward Island election has not come home true to the Cabinet or Members opposite. However, it will come true in the succeeding elections, both provincially and federally. Members of the Opposition might leave the wrong impression with a lot of people, particularly with inshore fishermen and potato producers, the people who depend on Atlantic waters to export their products.
I would like to point out that this Bill affects Canada shipping and services provided by the Coast Guard. That is important because many of the services provided in Atlantic Canada to fishermen are not provided by the Coast Guard. In fact, if one looks at the dredging services in our small craft harbours, one will find that those dredging services are provided by the Small Craft Harbours Branch of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans in fact contracts with the Department of Public Works to have dredging carried out. So the dredging services provided in most ports in Atlantic Canada have no involvement with the Coast Guard. I think it is unfortunate that Hon.
Canada Shipping Act
Members opposite have left the House with the impression that dredging services are going to be charged to the fishermen through the Coast Guard. In fact, that cannot happen because the Coast Guard does not provide that service to inshore fishermen in 99 per cent of harbours in Atlantic Canada. That is an important fact and I am concerned that the wrong impression might be left.
The suggestion has been made that if an inshore fisherman is out at sea and his boat breaks down, or perhaps he encounters heavy seas, his boat is swamped and he has to call for Coast Guard services for rescue of himself and perhaps his crew members, he will be hit with a major bill from the Coast Guard. We can assure this House that such would not be the case. I know this matter was discussed extensively in committee and assurances have been given that where safety of life and so on is involved, there would not be a charge back to the fisherman. I think I can stand here and assure fishermen in Atlantic Canada that if they are faced with an emergency, with a potential situation which involves lives, they will not be charged back for that service.
Certainly Hon. Members on this side of the House would not tolerate such a thing happening because safety of life is something about which we are all concerned. We would not let the Governor in Council, or whoever it may be, charge for that kind of thing, but the impression has been left that there would be a charge in that circumstance.
The Bill states that certain services "may" be charged for. Of course, there is a big difference between "may" and "will". They are two different words. This matter has been raised not only in the House of Commons committee but, as I understand it, in the Senate committee as well. Assurances have been given that no fishermen should hesitate to call for service. He is not going to be charged for that service which would be provided by the Coast Guard.
It has been suggested that we would be prepared to let our potato industry die because of services provided by the Coast Guard and so on. Again, I think it is absolutely incredible after the measures the Government has taken, even in recent months, that Opposition Members could suggest that we would let the kinds of fees be applied against the potato industry which would jeopardize that industry. In fact, just in the last few weeks potato producers in Prince Edward Island were assisted to the tune of $6 million from the federal Treasury to help them in a difficult period when potato prices were depressed. The Government had to come to the rescue in order to restore some market confidence. It had to take the potatoes out of the market so that market forces would prevail, supply and demand would raise prices, and that is exactly what has happened. Not only was help given in Prince Edward Island but I believe there has been $3 million worth of assistance given to the potato industry in New Brunswick. Therefore, the initiatives which have been taken and which are being taken daily suggests this Government's commitment to the primary producer, to the potato grower, to the fisherman and so on.

I am not aware of that Government ever taking the initiative to go out and talk to producers about guaranteeing services to ensure that they are effective for our primary producers. We are a long way from making the final decisions. We will have two years, just in terms of consultation, before that occurs.

GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ASSIST FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has always stood by the Canadian farmer. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced a series of initiatives which will provide immediate relief for hard-pressed Canadian food producers. The maximum allowable domestic price level of wheat has been raised to $11 per bushel. Effective today all federal taxes will be effectively eliminated on off-highway use of farm fuels. Farm debt review panel legislation will be dealt with on a priority basis.
These measures are very welcome news to western Canadian farmers and provide much needed assistance as they prepare for spring seeding. However, the long-term solutions for the farm economy lie in improved international trade. To that end the Prime Minister is meeting today with farm leaders in Vancouver to seek their advice and support before he leaves for the Tokyo Economic Summit. In Tokyo he will aggressively pursue the interests of Canadian farmers. The farmers of western Canada are getting the assistance they so urgently need, and the Government will continue to act on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to apologize for having inadvertently misled the House yesterday when I congratulated the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for having removed the sales and excise taxes

May 1, 1986
on farm fuels, and for his decision to allow domestic wheat prices to rise to $11 per bushel. Upon checking with officials, I have discovered that the Government is not removing sales and excise taxes, but is simply providing rebates to farmers of most, but not all, of those taxes. I regret that Prime Ministerial statements are not more specific and direct, and that I have contributed to the spreading of information which was not as factual as it first appeared.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the House the current situation facing the Canadian wine industry. The industry is suffering and jobs are being lost for a number of reasons, primarily, however, as a result of the flood of subsidized European imports. This is unfortunate because the industry now produces an outstanding product.
Members of Parliament and members of the Public Service can help. The people of Canada now pay tens of millions of dollars to transport MPs and members of the Public Service across the country. Mr. Speaker, Jews the world over have been celebrating Passover, the festival of freedom and hope. We speak out for freedom for all who are so deprived. We speak particularly to the sad case of Soviet Jews deprived of their right to practise ancient traditions, learn about their own heritage, speak and write their own language
as others are permitted to do, and join their families here in the West.
We speak of Benjamin Bogomolny and his wife Tanya awaiting Soviet permission to emigrate from Moscow in order to join his sister in Montreal. In Berne a conference on family reunification is currently under way. I urge the Canadian Government, through Ambassador Bauer, to press most vigorously for the reunification of the Bogomolny family and of other such families with members in Soviet bloc countries who wish to join their families here.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) has submitted a detailed presentation to me on the matter which she has already raised in the House. May I take this opportunity of commending the Hon. Member for Hamilton East on the manner in which she presented her written submission to me as it does provide all the information on which she seeks to base her case.
Before ruling, however, I should like to clear up what appears to be a misunderstanding. The Hon. Member first raised this question on the assumption that it was a matter arising out of the Question Period. Although the matter was referred to during the Question Period, there was no allegation that a breach of privilege had actually occurred during the Question Period. In such cases, a written notice of the kind which the Hon. Member has prepared is the proper method of giving the Chair notice of the question of privilege which is desired to be raised and which does not, therefore, arise directly from proceedings in the House. Contrary to some views, there are in fact no grounds for assuming that the question cannot be handled openly only because the submission is in writing.
With regard to the issue itself, the Hon. Member asserts that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) has improperly monitored communications between Members of Parliament and the Assistant Deputy Registrar General with the intention of interfering in the exercise of their duties and attempting to intimidate them. She bases her complaint on the fact that the Deputy Prime Minister had informed himself that communications had taken place between certain Members and the
Business of the House
Assistant Deputy Registrar General and on the fact that the latter had informed another Hon. Member that it was not the policy of his office to tell third parties who has consulted him. The Chair must decide whether these facts constitute prima facie evidence of a breach of privilege.
The precedents quoted by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East relate to the invasion of a Member's privacy within the precincts of Parliament, the interception of private communications including mail, electronic eavesdropping on a caucus meeting, and the unauthorized interrogation of a Member and her staff by the police. I must say that I can find nothing in the acts complained of which bear any relevance to the precedents she has quoted.
The fact that the Deputy Prime Minister has inquired whether Members of Parliament have been in communication with the Assistant Deputy Registrar General does not seem to me to constitute an interception of those communications. The fact that the Assistant Deputy Registrar General made a statement with regard to the policy of his office does not constitute evidence of a prima facie breach of privilege either.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton East includes in her submission a quotation from Erskine May's 19th Edition to the effect that any act or omission which obstructs or impedes a Member in the performance of his or her functions may be treated as a contempt of the House. Here we have the essence of the matter. If an Hon. Member is impeded or obstructed in the performance of his or her parliamentary duties through threats, intimidation, bribery attempts or other improper behaviour, such a case would fall within the limits of parliamentary privilege. Should an Hon. Member be able to say that something has happened which prevented him or her from performing functions, that he or she has been threatened, intimidated, or in any way unduly influenced, there would be a case for the Chair to consider. I cannot see that the Hon. Member's ability to perform her parliamentary functions have been impaired in any way. I am, therefore, unable to accord this matter precedence over other business.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for using this vehicle, Parliament, in the form of a statement in order to allow all three political Parties to respond to the same crisis in the international world caused by the accident at the nuclear reactor in the Soviet Union. I would like to applaud him for the efforts he has used to make sure the health of Canadians involved in the immediate vicinity will be monitored.
I feel the Canadian Government should be taking this one step forward. I have talked to a number of Canadians since the incident occurred and their concern is that we now live in a very interdependent world and that Russia, simply by the fact that it has had such a massive campaign of switching over their energy supplies to the nuclear field, has a responsibility that goes beyond the borders of the Soviet Union.
We, as a Canadian Government, because of our past involvement with United Nations agencies, should be taking a more positive step forward. I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to take it one step further and ask the Canadian Government to push the UN agencies in Vienna so that in the future there would be a much better response by the international community to the problems that occurred as a result of the crisis in the Soviet Union. The fact that it took several days after the accident before the rest of the world was informed of this crisis says something for the system by which we monitor atomic reactors throughout the world, whether it is behind the Iron Curtain or in the free world.
As the Minister knows, Canadian technology in this field has put us in the position of being a leader in this area of technology. I would hope that the Minister would instruct the task force he has set up internally to go beyond simply monitoring and assisting Canadians who were in the vicinity of the accident. We should avail ourselves of the opportunity to instruct the task force to review and tighten the regulations here in Canada, and perhaps look at the preventive measures that are in place.
The one thing that is going to be a fall out, if you will-and it is a play on words-from the nuclear accident in Russia will be the request by the Canadian public that we make sure our agencies which exist here in Canada can do an effective monitoring job, can enforce proper preventive care so we can prevent this kind of accident from occurring, not only in Canada but elsewhere in the world.
That is why I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare will instruct the task force to not only do an internal
Statements by Ministers
review of the way in which we react here in Canada but, more importantly, to use our traditional role on the world stage to ensure that the United Nations takes a major role in preventing this kind of occurrence from happening again in the future so that we will never again have to rely on sporadic news reports from other parts of the world to determine our own health and safety.
There should be presentations made to the Russian Government, not only here in Canada but through our United Nations agencies, outlining our concerns about the way in which they reacted to this accident. Canadians deserve, as do world citizens, to know more about what is happening to their health and safety as a result of this accident than what the Soviet Union has exhibited to date.

In any event, people are asking questions about travel plans and I hope they do not have to rely on the hot line. Yesterday, I phoned that hot line myself but the information I received was very unclear. Perhaps it has improved since then, but people on that phone did not know it was a hot line and simply replied that they would get back to me. I hope that service has been improved.
Perhaps the Minister can be excused for not addressing the very important point raised by the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). We live on a very small planet and no matter on what side of the Iron Curtain we live, no one has any less responsibility for being accountable to his fellow human beings for the kind of poisons-radioactive materials in this case-that are let loose upon an ecosphere that we hold in common. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I say to the Soviet Union that this was a grand opportunity for them to live up to some of the rhetoric we have often heard from them about the international community. So far, the Soviet Union has failed miserably in living up to that rhetoric. I hope they will take the opportunity to improve their reputation in the days ahead because we will be responding to this crisis for some time to come. I hope that what little we have to say in the House of Commons might encourage the Soviet Union to be more responsible about giving information than it has been in the last few days.
Finally, Members who have been here for some time know that since I came to the House in 1979 I have been asking the Canadian Government through every means I have had at my disposal to reconsider Canada's commitment to the nuclear energy option. We have a responsibility to look into our own back yard and conduct an inquiry into the whole nuclear fuel cycle in Canada. The Progressive Conservative Party promised to do that in 1979, but after some 18 months in office it has not lived up to that commitment.
In conclusion, I am sorry if it seems as if I were ending my remarks on a partisan note. However, that is not the case. The question of nuclear energy crosses many ideological boundaries as shown by the commitment to nuclear power of both the Soviet Union and the United States. They are taking chances with the world's environment for the sake of short term industrial and economic goals. They are taking an incredible risk with humanity and I believe it is time that Canada gave second thought to the impetus and encouragement it has given to the proliferation of nuclear reactors all over the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by repeating the thrust of my earlier remarks in the debate on Clause 4 of Bill C-75. Members will know that Clause 4 enacts a new section, Section 3.1, to the Canada Shipping Act and provides for charges related to the navigational services by the Canadian Coast Guard.
The point that I wanted to make in my earlier remarks is that Clause 4, new Section 3.1 of the Canada Shipping Act, relates to marine transportation. In fact, the whole thesis of the Canadian Shipping Act is marine transportation. It only incidentally and indirectly involves the coastal fisheries.
Members of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party would have Canadians believe that the whole thrust and purpose of this provision is to impose fees and charges on the fishermen of Canada, particularly those in the Atlantic area. That really is an illusion created by the Opposition. The purpose of the Canada Shipping Act and the amendments thereto are to ensure safety and fair competition on the oceans in relation to marine transportation.
I want to reiterate that because I do not want people to be misled by the remarks of opposition Members who try to portray and characterize these new provisions as having an adverse effect on those who travel the seaways in ships and vessels. That is absolutely not the purpose of this legislation. Canadians can put their minds to rest. Let them not listen to the arcane development of ideas and processes by members of the Opposition. We are here to increase safety on the oceans. We are here to advance the cause of marine transportation for Canada and Canadians.
It was interesting to listen to representations by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) in Ontario and by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), who represents an area of the Rideau Canal. I can understand their lack of knowledge as well as the frustration of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), when those Members talk about marine transportation in the narrow context in which they view this international activity that brings millions of dollars of revenue into Canada and employs thousands of Canadians on the East and
May 1, 1986

West Coast. Marine transportation is a major source of employment in the City of Halifax.
It grieves me to hear a Member, whose constituency includes the Rideau Canal, talk in serious terms about marine transportation. I can understand why the Member for Nickel Belt confuses this enormous subject of marine transportation with vague remarks about its effect on the fishery.
Let me enlighten those Members by referring to a presentation made by the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission when it appeared before the legislative committee. This is what it said in support of Clause 4 of Bill C-75:
Since 1964, when the St. Lawrence River was opened to year-round shipping activity, the Federal Government has spent considerable amounts of taxpayers' dollars to keep the river navigable.
Shipping lines serving inland Canadian markets via St. Lawrence River ports, benefit from the free provision of navigational services.
At the same time, competing shipping lines serving Halifax require extensive rail service to the same inland markets and have to pay the full inland cost by rail at compensatory rates.
Do we hear the Member for Nickel Belt complaining about that? Does the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier argue against that? No.
As the Ports Commission says, we are talking about the subsidization of the all-water route to Montreal in competition with the inland rail route from Halifax which is user pay. The fact that the Port of Halifax has to pay the full cost represents a government-created economic distortion between Halifax and Montreal. The purpose of this Bill is to address that distortion. I defy any Member from Atlantic Canada, including the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), to stand in the House and say that Atlantic Canada and the Port of Halifax do not benefit from this kind of provision. Our fear is that it will not be acted upon because of the misrepresentations made by Hon. Members from central Canada, aided and abetted by unknowing Hon. Members from Atlantic Canada. They seize the opportunity to distort the provisions of this Bill and try to fool the fishing industry. In that way they distort the whole process and do a disservice to Atlantic Canada and to all its residents.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear the comments made by the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). He seems to be taking the attitude that Hon. Members on this side of the House somehow or other oppose this Bill when in fact we on this side have supported the Bill in every way and have expedited its passage.
The only clause on which there has been a great difference of opinion is Clause 4. Clause 4 seeks to impose fees for all kinds of services which are rightfully provided by the Government of Canada, that is, the Coast Guard service, navigational aids and so on. I would point out to the Hon. Member for Halifax West that we are very conscious that Halifax is a major port. However, he should, by the same token, be
Canada Shipping Act
conscious that the Seaway is very important to my constituency of Algoma. We have the St. Mary's River and more tonnage goes through that river every year, which requires ice breaking and navigational services, than is trans-shipped through the Port of Halifax. I am not in any way putting down the massive responsibility of the Port of Halifax, but the Hon. Member seems to be trying to say that no one should talk about this subject but Members of Parliament from Halifax. It is very important to my constituency of Algoma. We need a lot of navigational aid and a lot of assistance from the Coast Guard. If the Government is going to take on to itself the power to impose charges for all kinds of things for which it has never charged in the past, members of the Opposition have every right to object.
I was interested to hear the comments of the Hon. Member for Cardigan (Mr. Binns). It seemed to me he took the same kind of approach as the Hon. Member for Halifax West. He seemed to be saying: "Look. As long as I am there, you don't have to worry about the Minister of Transport imposing those charges". I am sure that if the potato producers in Prince Edward Island were asked their opinion they would say: "Yes, that is what you told us last year, but then the Government imposed service charges for inspection of our potato crops". The people in Prince Edward Island showed just how much they were ready to trust the Government, both federally and provincially, in the last provincial election.
I would like to refer to some comments made by the National Farmers Union when it appeared before the committee on February 13.1 quote from its submission as follows:
Nonetheless farmers face in Section 4 of Bill C-75 proposals for further indirect taxation of their income already seriously battered by high production costs, rising interest rates, declining world prices, poor crops in some areas and protective trading and farm policies in many parts of the world, particularly in the U.S.
In its preoccupation to trim the federal deficit the Government is, in effect, telling farmers that the national interest can best be served by still further increasing farm costs at a time when the Farm Credit Corporation estimates that one in every four, or about 40,000 farmers in Canada with $20,000 or more in gross annual farm sales is in severe financial distress. The added costs to farmers implied by the new cost recovery proposals in Bill C-75 will provide nothing to enhance service in the movement of farm products that is not now offered and will only further impoverish farmers.
That is the kind of expression of concern we are hearing from the National Farmers Union. The Potato Marketing Board, on behalf of the Prince Edward Island potato industry, submitted its position paper on Clause 4 on February 13. The board in its submission stated, and I quote:
The P.E.I. potato industry supports the federal Government's policy on encouraging international trade. Thus we are vigorously opposed to the introduction of charges relating to navigational services until an impact study on the potato industry's export business is conducted.
I do not feel that the two members of the Government, who are obviously trying to cover up what powers the Government is taking onto itself, really do themselves much credit when we look at the briefs which were presented by their local organizations. We can certainly see that there is a great deal of concern. That is why we would like to see Clause 4 removed or at least made available for review in two years' time. The

May 1, 1986
Adjournment Motion
clause is totally sweeping. It is an enabling legislation which will allow the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to charge user fees for ice breaking services and navigational aids. When he asks for these powers he does not say how they will be used. There is no schedule to show what the charges will be, when they will be used and to whom they will apply.
In many parts of the shipping industry we see higher levies, but at the same time we see a decrease in the use of the Seaway. The additional charges which will be imposed under Clause 4 will discourage just that much more the use of this most important inland waterway. I think Clause 4 really requires a great deal of further consideration.
We are not only talking about services for the commercial vessels which go through the Seaway or ply the coasts of Canada, we are as well looking at the internal waterways of this country. In my constituency fishing is a relatively important industry. We are situated on the shores of Lake Superior and on the north shore of Lake Huron and Manitoulin Island. Our fishermen certainly require the services of the Coast Guard and navigational aids and assistance. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, their position is not such that they can pay for additional services. That is why we are urging the Government to withdraw this clause.
We agree with the Bill. We realize the legislation is out of date and needs to be updated. We want to see it passed, but without Clause 4 which is totally unacceptable to the Opposition and I suspect to many of the government back-benchers in the quiet and privacy of their caucus room. Here on the floor of the House of Commons they have to knuckle under the pressure put on them by the Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), who always steps on the back-benchers. He does not allow them to bring forth their own ideas and prevents them from speaking honestly and fairly. They should be allowed to express the concerns of the potato producers and fishermen in the small craft harbours throughout the Great Lakes and on both coasts. Clause 4 is totally unacceptable and must be withdrawn.

On top of that, today is the first day that these same fishermen who may be charged for their icebreaker, for navigational aids or for any number of things by the Government are being charged to tie boats up to a government wharf owned either by Small Craft Harbours, the Department of Transport or the Department of Public Works.

The Government turns around and says: "Well, the charge is not very much. It is only $ 1 a day if you have a 45-foot boat". A dollar a day three months in advance is $100. Who is this money to be collected by? It will be collected by someone on social assistance or on unemployment insurance who is told that he can keep 70 per cent of what he collects on the first $1,000, and then the formula goes down. the Association's Chairman of the Board, Mr. Runciman, wrote a letter to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), in which he said: Dear Prime Minister-and, among other things:

-in the opinion of our members, the Government does not need all the power it is seeking via Clause 4 to achieve its announced objective. Mr. Speaker, we are very concerned, not that we are any less Canadian because we are proud Quebecers, but we are well aware of the struggle that has been going on for years to be able to keep our ports open year-round.
I am thinking about us Montrealers. Surely the Members who represent the Halifax area will understand that we too want to put up a strong defence on behalf of the ridings we represent.

I agree that the principle in itself is justifiable, particularly in times of economic hardships when all Governments- provincial, municipal and federal alike-are strapped for cash. So the Government wants to boost its revenues as much as possible.
But must this be considered as being fair to all classes of society? A moment ago my colleague the Hon. Member from the Province of Newfoundland told us that beginning today . ..
Canada Shipping Act
what a surprise, May 1, usually the occasion to celebrate workers the world over. Well if we consider that fishermen are workers, this is their celebration and on that very occasion we are told that, beginning today, even in the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), any fisherman who wants to use a federal pier to moor his boat will have to pay, if I understood correctly what my colleague said. He is indignant because there had never been any question about that since his province joined the rest of Canada. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are quite a few fishermen in eastern Canada. I do not really understand the attitude of the Government. If these amendments were accepted, the Bill would go through. However, the Government has insisted upon including Clause 4, and insisted that we must accept or reject the Bill as a whole. That is sad. Much of what is contained in the Bill is acceptable, but the Government is being stubborn and wants to include Clause 4, the one dealing with user fees, even after many protests by the Great Lakes Waters Development Association and its membership, as well as many representations from the Montreal Chamber of Commerce and others. The Minister wants to be given a blank cheque. I do not think my Party or the NDP want to give the Minister a blank cheque so that user fees can be charged. He said: Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say concerning the amendments proposed by the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin). The amendments arise from the report on the Ocean Ranger disaster and the actions of the Government to date regarding those recommendations. When one examines the actual amendments, one discovers that the main points raised in the amenments have to do with the jurisdiction of the federal Government over drilling rigs in one way or the other. In other words, as things presently exist on the drilling rigs offshore, there are at least two jurisdictions as far as safety is concerned: first, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney); second, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski); and we could add a third jurisdiction, that being a provincial authority. In the case of the Province of Newfoundland, perhaps there could be an agreement between both Governments to have joint jurisdiction, but certainly we should have provincial regulations set down by the provincial petroleum authority. There is perhaps a fourth jurisdiction involved, and that is the international code or the building standards from which the rig originates or where the rig was built.
Under this Bill certainly, safety standards are tightened up as far as the construction of vessels or oil drilling rigs in Canada is concerned, but it does not address the question of an oil rig from the United States, from some part of Europe or from some other part of the world that is presently drilling just

outside the 200 mile limit, say in Hibernia. It does not cover those particular oil drilling rigs.
That opens up perhaps another question relevant to these amendments, and that is the extension of jurisdiction of the Canada Shipping Act to cover areas outside of the present jurisdiction of 200 miles. It also raises the question, as was raised in the Ocean Ranger report, of who is in charge of a vessel. Under the Canada Shipping Act, it is the captain. If you visit an oil rig, you will find that there is perhaps a mixed jurisdiction between the so-called captain and the tool pusher, who is in charge of the drilling that actually takes place on that rig. That is the foundation for the three amendments proposed by the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port- St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin).
When one reads the report on the Ocean Ranger one can see why the Hon. Member from Newfoundland is so concerned about these amendments. One could not read the report without wondering what is wrong with our present system of monitoring activities and allocating jurisdictions with regard to safety aboard these drilling rigs on Canada's offshore. One wonders why none of the 20 to 30 people, who were alive in the water and threw a line aboard a rescue ship, were saved, especially with helicopters on site. A line was thrown aboard the so-called stand-by vessel which was supposed to be carrying out search and rescue activities as part of its operation as a stand-by supply vessel. One wonders how a line could be thrown aboard that ship from the people in the boat without those people being saved.
That is the foundation of the amendments moved by the Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe. The basic question asked by the Hon. Member in this Chamber through these amendments goes unanswered. It has not been responded to by the Government of Canada. The Royal commission report and the follow-up reports explained exactly what went wrong. All of the recommendations were submitted after the present Government took office. The Government of Canada can say that it has instituted 85 per cent of the recommendations made in the royal commission report. That does not, however, address the basic question of who has jurisdiction in the offshore. It cannot be divided between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Transport, the Provincial Petroleum Directorate, and the United States Shipping Standards.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join in the debate on the amendments moved by the Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin). The amendments before the House are identical in purpose to those moved in committee by me. These amendments would clearly outline that the responsibility for the safety of people who work on mobile offshore drilling units is in the hands of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). I give the Government credit for moving on the interpretation of the area of responsibility. If my memory is correct, we moved from strict jurisdiction by the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Resources to jurisdiction split between the Ministry of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Ministry of Transport.
Unlike the debate on Clause 4, through which we tried to restrict the powers of the Minister of Transport, through this amendment moved by the Liberal Party we want to increase the powers of that Minister. We do so out of recognition that with regard to matters dealing with a vessel, which for all intents and purposes a mobile offshore drilling unit is, it should be under the strict control of the master of that vessel. The jurisdiction should not be shared with the person who has knowledge of how to extract resources from the sea but, rather, should be the sole responsibility of the person who knows the ocean, the currents, and the seaworthiness of the drilling unit of which he or she is in charge.
This issue arises out of the very unfortunate sinking of the Ocean Ranger. I would like to quote briefly from that report as it relates to the issue at hand. It reads:
May 1, 1986

It is instructive to note, however, the general trend towards a lead agency, if not a "single window", for regulatory purposes.
The United Kingdom has adopted the single agency approach in allocating full responsibility to the Department of Energy, and Norway has initiated the process of moving full responsibility to the Petroleum Directorate... .In Canada the principle of a single window approach was adopted by the establishment of the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration (COGLA). It is recommended:
86.	That Canada maintain the approach of a single regulatory agency, in concept and in practice, in exercising regulatory control over MODUs and the varied aspects of their drilling operations including the standby role of vessels and the rescue role of helicopters under contract to industry.
A device common to all jurisdictions under review to ameliorate jurisdictional jealousies, administrative overlaps and lack of co-ordination is the Memorandum of Understanding negotiated between the lead agency or single window agency and another department or agency-In Canada, the Memorandum of Understanding has been used for transferring powers in the reverse direction, as, for example, the empowering of the Canadian Coast Guard, through delegation from COGLA, to undertake certain functions that would otherwise be outside their jurisdiction.
It is suggested that this practice be reversed. If the single regulatory agency referred to in Recommendation 86 is to have the authority and capability to exercise fully the responsibilities envisaged for it in Recommendation 80, then powers, and in some cases personnel, will need to be transferred to it. It is recommended:
87.	That powers and, where necessary, personnel be transferred by Memoranda of Understanding to the single regulatory agency from other line departments and government agencies so that it can exercise fully and effectively its responsibility for safety of MODUs and the varied aspects of their drilling operations including the standby role of vessels and the rescue role of helicopters under contract to industry.
While the presentations made to the legislative committee with this matter were very small relative to the number that were made on the matter of Clause 4, the cost recovery clause, there was consistency throughout. Everyone who came before us said that there should be one agency. They said quite clearly that it should be the Minister of Transport who is responsible ultimately. Therefore, it would be the master on the MODU who would have responsibility in a time of crisis to make the decisions as to the safety of staying where they were, or whether, in fact, they should pull up their anchor and the pipes and get to an area of the ocean that is safe for both the people on the equipment and the equipment itself. The company of Master Mariners of Canada in a letter to the Minister of Transport wrote the following:
The Sea is an exacting mistress and Safety at Sea will be severely compromised should the use of uncertified and probably inexperienced personnel be allowed to take charge of Drilling rigs and Offshore supply vessels. There is no substitute for an experienced and well qualified seaman.
I think that sums it up. It makes the point that we should give the Minister of Transport the power to have jurisdiction. He should not have to negotiate with the Minister of Energy. He should have the power and ability to decide what is needed for the safety and the protection of those people on the rigs. I would encourage the Government to move that one more step and to accept this amendment.
