PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   NATURAL RESOURCES GRAND CANAL WATER DIVERSION PROJECT
speechtext:
That:
Whereas certain Canadian private interest groups are seriously proposing the Grand Canal project, which would involve constructing a dike across Janies Bay and diverting water to the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence water basin through a system of canals, dams, underground water tunnels and pumping stations, for sale and redistribution to arid regions of the United States; and
Whereas the Grand Canal project is looked upon favourably by the Prime Minister of Canada, Premier of Quebec, Canadian Free Trade Negotiator Simon Reisman and other public officials; and
Whereas concern has been expressed that Canadian fresh water may be included in free trade negotiations with the United States; and
Whereas there has been no consideration given to the impacts of the Grand Canal project on the enviornment and on the native population of the James Bay area whose livelihood depends on this water resource; and
Whereas proposed government studies of the Grand Canal project are contradictory to the goals and objectives of the 1985 Great Lakes Charter and a long-standing Canadian Government policy against mass water exports.
Now, therefore, be it resolved, that this House expresses its outrage that the Grand Canal project could be seriously considered by Canadian private interest groups and public officials and opposes any study or further consideration of the proposal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I suppose that at any moment we will be faced with the usual interruption from the Senate in order
that we go down to witness Royal Assent in the Senate Chamber. I hope that will happen sometime after I finish my speech and not before.
In any event, I wish to speak about the Grand Canal scheme which is the brain-child of a Newfoundland-based engineer, Thomas Kierens, who proposes to build a dam across James Bay, thereby preventing fresh water from the James Bay watershed from flowing into Hudson Bay, eventually turning James Bay into a huge fresh water lake. This fresh water would then be rediverted south through a system of canals, tunnels and pumping stations to the Great Lakes, and beyond to points in the mid-west and southwest United States. At an estimated cost of $100 billion to $200 billion, the Grand Canal would be the most expensive construction project in Canadian history and would be a truly massive undertaking.
Mass water diversion and export proposals such as the Grand Canal are not new. Diversion schemes involving James Bay date back to the 1930s and several water diversion and export projects in western Canada have also been proposed, most notably the North American Water and Power Alliance or NAWAPA project. In the past, these proposals were considered too bizarre to be accorded much credibility. Lately, however, this situation has apparently changed and the Grand Canal has been given unsettling credibility in certain circles.
Kierens and his company, Grandco, have managed to line up an impressive number of influential people to back the Grand Canal scheme including Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa; Louis Desmarais, a former Liberal MP and brother of Paul Desmarais, the Chairman of Power Corporation; Bechtel Canada, the builders of the James Bay project and a subsidiary of the largest engineering firm in the world; and Canada's free trade negotiator, Simon Reisman, to name but a few. Many of these groups and individuals have been quietly lobbying the Government to support the Grand Canal project and to fund studies of the scheme. Grandco has already received a $30,000 grant from the St. John's office of the National Research Council and the NRC, and other government Departments are currently studying another request for an additional $750,000 for a pre-feasibility study of the scheme.
In the face of this lobbying, not to mention persistent questions by myself and others who are concerned about this issue, the Government has taken a curiously vacillating and inconsistent approach to the whole question. On the one hand, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said recently that any decision on mass water diversion or export schemes would have to await the formulation of a national water policy. He also added that he is personally opposed to the Grand Canal scheme and other inter-basin transfers of water. On the other hand, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has not only endorsed the export of water by tanker from his own riding but he was also quoted in Fortune magazine of March of last year
May 1, 1986

as saying something to the effect that he would be willing to consider mass water exports to the United States.
Then last April 19, in response to a question put by the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), the Prime Minister indicated his support for the Grand Canal when he said the following:
I want to give my hon. friend the assurance that I view the prospect with enthusiasm. In fact, I can tell him that I am working on draft terms of reference whereby the federal Government might properly involve itself in co-operation with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador and the Government of Quebec in developing these kinds of resources for the benefit of the citizens of those two provinces and Canada.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister of Canada speaking in this House, and his comments cannot be misconstrued or attributed to comments made before the last election as the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tried to imply when I asked a question on this matter on January 22.
Tonight, hopefully someone from the government benches will clarify for the House just who, the Prime Minister or the Minister of the Environment, speaks for the Government on the Grand Canal and on water exports in general. If it is the Prime Minister, perhaps the government spokesperson could also explain what happened to the terms of reference to which the Prime Minister referred last year and why the Government has abandoned a long-standing Canadian policy against water export schemes such as the Grand Canal.
We also need clarification from the Liberal Party. On one hand, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) appears to be genuinely opposed to the Grand Canal and other mass water export schemes. On the other, as I have already noted, at least one influential former Liberal MP, the current Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, and the Liberal Premier of Quebec appear to be enthusiastically supportive of the Grand Canal. For his part, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), when I asked him about his position on the Grand Canal, merely said that he thought it should be studied. The Liberals are obviously of two minds on water exports and the Grand Canal just as they are on other issues like free trade and universality.
This leads me to another concern I and others have about the Grand Canal and similar water export schemes. In recent months, Simon Reisman, Canada's free trade negotiator and a vocal proponent of the Grand Canal, has not only said on numerous occasions that Canada's fresh water should be on the free trade negotiating table but has gone as far as to say that allowing American access to Canadian fresh water may, in fact, be a cornerstone of any free trade agreement with the United States. The Secretary of State has said that Canadian water is not on the bargaining table and has even gone as far as to be irritated with me for asking the question more than once. Yet Mr. Reisman voices his personal views with sufficient regularity and the Government, particularly the Prime Minister, is sufficiently vague on water exports that one cannot help but be worried.
Grand Canal Project
Canadian waters are not ours to sell, Mr. Speaker. In this sense, opposition to the Grand Canal and other water export schemes is not to be seen as selfishness but as good stewardship of that which has been entrusted to us. Furthermore, the inclusion of Canadian water in free trade negotiations with the United States would pose serious consequences for Canadian sovereignty. Unlike other resource projects, once something like the Grand Canal is in place, Canada cannot just decide to turn off the tap. No mater what, Canada will be obliged to keep the water flowing. That is the simple, hard fact of the matter. What is more, once one diversion scheme like the Grand Canal is in place, a precedent will be established. Not only might the Americans come to expect ready access to Canadian fresh water but Canadians, particularly under Tory or Liberal Governments, might feel obliged or pressured to deliver. This one precious resource could draw Canadians inextricably into the already stifling embrace of the United States. For those of us who value this country and would like to see Canada pursue independent foreign, domestic and environmental policies, mass water export schemes such as the Grand Canal must be resisted.
What about the social cost, Mr. Speaker? The Grand Canal project would entail a massive disruption and dislocation of northern communities due to a rapid escalation in development. Particularly hard hit would be native Canadians whose traditional lifestyle would be severely compromised. Furthermore, should the grand Canal project go ahead, it would place a multitude of obstacles in the path of equitable Indian land claims settlements and Indian self-government.
We have seen far too often in the past that Indian rights invariably take second place to mega-projects and there is no reason to believe that the Grand Canal would be any different. This is no doubt one of the reasons the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation, which represents 42 northern Ontario Indian bands and whose Grand Chief I had the opportunity to meet recently, has been one of the most vocal opponents of the Grand Canal.
In a telex objecting to the Grand Canal that the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation and Great Lakes United sent to the Prime Minister on February 10, the Nishnawbi-Aski Nation outlined its concerns clearly when it noted the following:
Your government has brought into question the strength of constitutional guarantees for the Nishnawbe-Aski peoples' aboriginal and treaty rights.
Doubt has been cast on the seriousness with which your government will support Indian self-government initiatives and the future Indian control of resources.
These are legitimate concerns and all of us in the House have an obligation to resist any efforts to further degrade and abuse the rights and land of Canada's aboriginal people.
Finally, there are the environmental consequences of the Grand Canal to consider. The most obvious of these would be the scars on the landscape and environment in general that would result after an army of engineers and construction workers had blasted, hacked and carved their way through the Canadian Shield in building the various dams, canals, tunnels and pumping stations necessary to create a man-made lake at

May 1, 1986
Grand Canal Project
James Bay and to transport the resulting fresh water. Another obvious environmental consequence would be that the Grand Canal would condemn to destruction the entire marine ecosystem in and around James Bay including all the fish, seals, whales, sea birds, vegetation and other living organisms that depend on a saltwater environment to survive.
It is also believed that this project could seriously affect global climatic conditions by blocking the flow of fresh water that flows into James Bay and on into Hudson Bay and the Arctic Ocean. Scientists fear that the Grand Canal, by shutting off James Bay, would increase salinity levels in Hudson Bay and the Arctic Ocean thereby melting icebergs and the polar ice cap and increasing temperatures in the Arctic. If this were to happen, weather conditions around the northern hemisphere could be permanently altered, affecting agricultural and other important social and economic activities. What a prospect: if the Grand Canal were to go ahead in the rush to find a quick fix, a technocratic solution to irrigation problems south of the border and economic problems here in Canada, we could in fact destroy countless acres of productive land around the world.
Another aspect of the Grand Canal is one I have raised on numerous occasions, including this afternoon, and that is, nuclear energy. The backers of the Grand Canal are considering using nuclear power to pump water from James Bay down to the Great Lakes. Atomic Energy of Canada admitted recently that it is already studying the feasibility of using nuclear power in connection with the Grand Canal scheme. According to Energy Probe, the Grand Canal Scheme would require 12,500 megawatts of generating capacity, a power demand that equals half the demand of the Province of Ontario at peak hours. To provide this power, one would need more power than is available from the entire James Bay project or, worse, 17 Bruce-sized nuclear reactors.
As one who has long opposed nuclear power and the underhanded nature in which the nuclear industry operates, I am hardly surprised that AECL sees a great opportunity here. AECL is always looking for an excuse to justify its nuclear reactor program. However, as we have seen this week as a result of the tragic nuclear accident in Ukraine-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on this motion moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). He and I see eye to eye because of our height, and we also see eye to eye on this particular motion.
Large scale water transfer projects, such as we have already seen in Canada, are a technical possibility with sometimes undesirable environmental and social consequences. In the rush to meet increasing water demands for energy, agriculture and other needs, we often tend to forget that the development, management and regulation of our own water heritage must correspond with ecological realities. Technical feasibility and socioeconomic gain can no longer be promoted at the expense of ignoring environmental issues. A planner's perspective must now transcend what is technically and economically feasible, socially and politically acceptable and legally permissible, to include the consideration of ecological constraints and consequences of water resource development. Canadians no longer tolerate ecological naivete, and neither will the Government, especially when it applies to land use for embassies in Ottawa which may impact on the fresh water of the Ottawa River.
Public reaction to such recent domestic water projects as the Slave River Hydro Development, Skagit, Garrison Diversion and others, when they appeared to threaten ecosystem stability, was immediate and vociferous. Public reaction does not stop after flagging the issues. For example, in the case of the James Bay Project, the first environmental impact studies based on new research were undertaken, not by developers but by independent scientists working on behalf of native groups and funded by the federal Government.
Technological advances and a gradual progression northward in search of suitable sites for damning or diversion have led to the recent advocation of megaprojects. Disadvantages of such proposals are often found in the inherent complexity of the projects themselves. Their large size increases the potential interaction between project components and the ecosystem. For these large projects our understanding of all the components and links are often incomplete. Unfortunately, the aspects which are studied are those which address short-term concerns.
It would appear, therefore, that as the magnitude of such projects increases with greater influence on the biosphere, so does the inaccuracy and uncertainty of being able to predict the project's environmental consequences. Also, inadequate lead time for study and research of the project-environment relationship has, on occasion, resulted in a failure to anticipate major ecological changes outside the sphere of influence of the development. Operation of the W.A.C. Bennett damn, for example, resulted in major adverse changes to prime marsh habitat 800 kilometers downstream of the damn site. That is quite remarkable, Mr. Speaker.
It seems, therefore, that the more drastic the changes in the river regime, the more extensive will be the expected disruption to the ecological balance. On occasion, such imbalances have led to direct economic hardships or health concerns as in the case of mercury contamination of commercially important downstream fisheries in the Churchill-Nelson system in Manitoba or reduction of the subsistence fishery in the La Grande River in Quebec.
May 1, 1986

On the other hand, we can rest assured that environmentally significant activities such as large scale water transfers will be subject to the full attention of the federal Government's regulatory apparatus and environmental protection mandate. In addition, guidelines, regulations and legislation protecting wildlife-in which I have a great personal, professional, and political interest-water quality, endangered species, environmentally sensitive regions and heritage rivers come into play in the planning, evaluation and implementation of such activities.
I am reminded that in 1969 I did a paper in the ecology class of Dr. Vaillancourt at the University of Ottawa in cooperation with a classmate, Cathi Campbell. I quote myself from that paper as follows: "The importance of our water resources will become immense before the end of the century".
Specifically, the federal environmental assessment and review process requires federal agencies to administer the process when proposed activities have federal involvement and may significantly affect the environment. An undertaking of such magnitude as water transfer would likely meet one or more of the criteria for federal involvement. If a review were to demonstrate environmental deficiencies in project planning, the construction of a water transfer project would not go forward until appopriate studies were completed and the deficiencies corrected.
Furthermore, should a review demonstrate the potential for major environmental damage, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has the final option, as part of the process, not to approve construction of the project. From this it can be seen that when projects of this magnitude come under government scrutiny, the federal Government retains a firm controlling hand. Environmental assessment in Canada has neither wisely used, nor demanded, post-development audit information for diversion schemes on which to build a predictive base for possible environmental impact assessment. Despite Canada's poor record of post-development auditing, certain general environmental issues can be suggested as requiring attention for water transfers of any consequence. Large scale diversions of northward flowing rivers that are proposed or under way on several continents have certain environmental impact features in common.
Inter-basin water transfers where two or more distinct drainages are involved retain the potential for biotic transfer. Invading fish species may replace more economically desirable ones or introduce parasites to previously isolated populations. Such biological changes may range from beneficial to totally catastrophic. I am reminded of what happened when eels infested our Great Lakes system which created a tremendous problem. A former professor of mine, also at the University of Ottawa, Dr. Vladikov, was instrumental in solving that problem.
When the riverine discharge to the sea is altered in quantity or timing, the resulting changes may cause dramatic shifts in the dynamics of coastal marine processes and organisms. Altering James Bay from salt to fresh water would most
Grand Canal Project
certainly cause complete changes in characteristics of the bay's wildlife with as yet unidentified far-reaching consequences.
Assessing the environmental impact of major diversion of northward flowing rivers is, at the present, speculative at best. Examination of analogous situations in the U.S.S.R. and our own experience with diversions, albeit of smaller magnitude, have raised the level of public and scientific concern. Longterm ecological and climatological effects, particularly major changes in Arctic ice pack formation, atmospheric circulation, temperature, and in precipitation patterns in the northern hemisphere are all within the realm of possibility. Even if we can convince ourselves that one project by itself does not cause measurable impact on such factors, we must look ahead and consider what the impact of separate projects in one country, or projects in several countries, will have.
For the Grand Canal scheme augmentation of existing data bases would be a necessary requirement in order to make realistic predictions of the potential effects of terminating the freshwater flow of James Bay into Hudson Bay. We know that a major ecosystem shift would follow the altering of James Bay from salt to fresh water and include the loss of salt marshes, an estuarine habitat important to a major portion of the North American migratory bird population. The understanding of the dynamics and economic cost of such changes remain, at present, out of reach until engineering scenarios are better defined and biological data bases completed.
The creation of "anti rivers" and hydrological pumping systems to transport the water south may also result in classical environmental problems of erosion, water quality, fish migration problems and habitat loss, etc., already associated with existing, less ambitious water transfer schemes. When reservoirs are introduced into the scheme of things as part of water transfer projects, those impacts normally associated with reservoir construction and operation also add to the projects over-all complexity, degree of environmental disturbance and need for mitigation.
Environmental concerns are no longer a "frill" in the minds of Canadians and must be taken very seriously. The Minister of the Environment has already indicated that more must be learned about the environmental effects of large-scale water diversions before we can proceed with implementation of any such scheme. Massive export and sale of our fresh water is not acceptable. As far as I am concerned it is not now and never should be-and God help us if it ever is-on the bargaining table.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this will be my first long speech in French in this House, I intend to use a written speech. I admit the speech was drafted by civil servants, but I trust you will find it both entertaining and edifying.

May 1, 1986
Grand Canal Project
In recent years, Canadians have become increasingly aware of the vital connection between the environment and the economy. As a result of this awareness, we now see a healthy and growing interest in our environmental resources. We know that economic growth and maintaining our economic perspectives require us to have pure air, clean water and good soil conditions. We know that like any prosperous merchant, we must take an inventory of our natural environment. Exhausting our natural resources, as a result of bad management and a thirst for profit, means that we compromise our prospects for the future. In a world that is becoming increasingly competitive, only careful management of our natural resources will give us an edge over our competitors.
Water is undoubtedly one of our most precious resources. In Canada we have become very much aware of our responsibility for maintaining the quantity and improving the quality of the water we have. Canadians understand more than ever before that careful management is essential if we are to transfer this resource intact to future generations.
In Canada, we are lucky to have an abundant supply of hydraulic resources. However, it is clear that vital elements of our economic well-being depend on a delicate balance between the reserves at our disposal and how we use them. In recent years, Western Canada experienced the devastating effects that insufficient precipitation can have on agriculture and forestry, and further east, the Great Lakes region suffered excessive precipitation which caused considerable damage to lakeshore property and serious economic problems. There is also the increasing problem of water pollution, caused either directly by spillage or indirectly by airborne pollution. Thus, even if it is an abundant resource, we cannot take it for granted. The time has come to act quickly to protect both quality and quantity.
This is a task that will have to be shared by all, by the federal Government and the provincial governments, by industry, cities and municipalities, by farmers and by all Canadians. Those who share the benefits must also share the responsibility for managing this resource. This will require a national consensus on the best way to manage and use this resource, while ensuring that it is improved and maintained for future generations of Canadians.
I think a step has already been made in the right direction. The Government is now looking at the findings and recommendations of the Pearse Commission whose mission it was to investigate our federal water policy. The Commission examined every aspect of the situation, from pollution to international agreements on management of international waterways. I think it is important to point out that the Commission examined the various management aspects of the question, while at the same time considering water as a complete and indivisible entity. I believe that in drafting a sound management policy we must continue to look upon this very precious resource as a whole rather than try to deal separately with one or the other aspect of its management.
I have already referred briefly to a number of serious problems facing Canadians with respect to the quality and quantity of available waters. I would suggest that priority will have to be given to a serious examination of the social, economic, intergovernmental, international, technical and environmental impact of current or proposed water uses because all these factors will influence the over-all and coherent management of this resource, and will in turn be influenced by the way it is managed. One of the earlier problems concerning water management was that, although we had the required technical know-how to build dams, hydro lines and waterways, or to develop new chemical products, we simply did not know how to minimize as quickly as possible the unforeseen and undesirable secondary effects such as social upheavals caused by community disruption, loss of a traditional means of survival, or again damages to the environment due to the destruction of spawning grounds, or water losses caused by industrial or agricultural pollution.
Oftentimes in the past the benefits derived from such activities were offset to various degrees by these secondary effects. Efforts were made as well to remedy certain situations, but in a number of cases they gave partial results only, or required much time, energy and money.
In my judgment, part of the problem was and still is our tendency to consider only the positive aspects of any new plan or development. The sound management of our water resources requires us to examine closely all factors which might have a direct or indirect impact on them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie): apologies accepted. The Hon. Member's Motion No. 104 deals with a very important issue of concern to many Canadians. I am glad that the Hon. Member has given us the opportunity this day to discuss the issue further.
Last year, the Priorities and Planning Committee of Cabinet empowered the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to act for the Government in formulating a national water policy. Indeed, the Minister has given this matter top priority. The Cabinet has further decided that until this policy is in place, there will be no major inter-basin diversions or large scale exports of water. Even then, any decision for or against water policy will be made in the context of an over-all policy and not on an ad hoc basis.
May 1, 1986

The first step in developing the water policy was the inquiry on federal water policy headed by Dr. Peter Pearse of the University of British Columbia. The Pearse inquiry was established in January, 1984, and reported to the Minister of the Environment in September, 1985.
The mandate of the Pearse inquiry was to consider the nature of emerging issues. These issues included the state of the water resource, future requirements for water, interjurisdictional dimensions and scientific and research expertise with a view to ensuring the enhancement of the health, wellbeing and prosperity of the people of Canada. In conducting its work, the inquiry actively sought the views of provincial, territorial and federal government departments and their agencies, of private citizens and public groups, as well as the input of industry and the academic community in Canada.
Between late September and early December, 1984, 201 presentations were heard at 33 days of hearings in 17 locations across Canada. Over 300 written submissions were received by the inquiry. In addition, the inquiry commissioned 22 separate research papers on special problems. Praise is due to the inquiry members for their wide and effective process of consultation.
Not surprisingly, one of the topics that generated keen interest in all parts of Canada was the issue of water export. Of the 77 briefs on this subject, most were opposed to the idea. Only a few, mainly the promoters of particular projects, regarded exports as a promising economic opportunity.
In its final report entitled Currents of Change, the inquiry made 55 recommendations. Three of these recommendations deal with the subject of water export. The inquiry concluded that:
It would be imprudent for the Federal Government to reject all exports out of hand.
The inquiry members went on to say that any water export policy: "Should clearly set out the conditions that must be met for any proposal to be acceptable", and that there should be: "Clear procedures for assessing export proposals." Therefore, in its conclusions, the inquiry recommended that:
The Federal Government should pass legislation to require anyone who proposes to export water to obtain a licence. This legislation should identify the matters that will be taken into account in considering a licence application.
Small scale export proposals, such as those involving tanker operations, were viewed in a different light than the inter-basin transfers to the United States because of the obvious differences in their impacts and the volumes of water involved. Because diversions for large scale water export to the United States, which would include proposals such as Grand Canal, require very careful scrutiny, the inquiry recommended that:
The Cabinet should determine whether the Government is prepared to consider large-scale diversions of water to the United States and, if so, the criteria that must be met for approval of proposals.
Further, if the Government is going to consider diversions to the United States, the Pearse inquiry recommended that for the purposes of assessing water export proposals having significant environmental, social or economic implications, the
Grand Canal Project
Minister of the Environment should be empowered to appoint a special review panel for each proposal. These panels should consist of members appointed in consultation with the governments of provinces or territories directly affected by the project.
Further, the panels should investigate the full range of matters that the Minister must review in considering an application for an export licence, according to criteria determined by government. Third, these panels should receive information and analysis from relevant governments and agencies, as well as from the proposal's proponents and other interested groups. Fourth, the panels should consider feasible modifications of the proposal in terms of scale, characteristics and time of construction.
Fifth, the panel should hold public hearings where no other suitable provisions are made for the public to review the implications for the interests of all Canadians. Finally, the panels should publicly report their findings, with recommendations about whether the licence should be granted and, if so, what terms and conditions should be attached to the particular licence.
The Pearse inquiry made two additional points on the export of water issue. First, applicants should bear the costs of assembling the information required for assessments, and the Government should not be doing their homework for them. Second, the Government should resist pressures to support any large international diversions, at least until recommended arrangements are in place.
This is exactly what the Government had been attempting to do. The Minister of the Environment has said publicly on many occasions that decisions on water export will not be made until a national water policy is in place.
Developing that water policy is now a top priority of the Government. Within a week of receiving the inquiry's report, the Hon. Minister of the Environment presented it to his provincial colleagues at the meeting of the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers. He requested their reaction within six months. In November, 1985, the Minister similarly met and discussed the report with about 300 representatives of the environmental, non-government organizations. Following this inquiry, the Minister also established an interdepartmental water policy task force to assist him in developing the new national water policy. The task force will be reviewing the inquiry's recommendations and taking into account the views of the provinces, the non-governmental organizations and the general public. This group will be advising him, this summer, on a course of action.
In developing that portion of a national water policy on large scale water exports, there clearly are a great number of issues that must be considered. For instance, transferring water from one watershed to another or one oceanic basin to another can have uncertain ecological effects. Diversions involve significant changes to the natural environment by interrupting river flows, flooding, the transferral of life forms

May 1, 1986
*

Grand Canal Project
and may even have the potential for changing atmospheric or oceanic conditions. These changes would impinge on land and other uses of natural resources and threaten to dislocate established communities that are dependent on them. Really, their environmental and social impacts must be considered irreversible for all practical purposes.
The question of capital investment must also be considered in such a discussion. It would be enormous and difficult to predict, given long construction periods. Moreover, capital costs could be recouped only over long operational periods. This presents additional uncertainties about cost, benefits and the future direction of technological change.
To aggravate the situation, there are the international dimensions of such large water diversion schemes. How do they fit into international law and established arrangements between Canada and the United States under existing treaties? The recent Great Lakes Charter, a statement of intent among the eight states and two provinces bordering the Great Lakes, is opposed to any diversion schemes. Perhaps the most important factor of which we must take note is the lack of demand at this time for our water. As the Hon. Minister of the Environment said: "The Americans are not beating down our door yet". In fact, we have not had official overtures from the United States or from any other country at this time for our water. The report of the inquiry states that: "Foreign demand on Canadian water is so far a made-in-Canada controversy". U.S. officials have continued to be indifferent to water importation schemes, which is in marked contrast to the heated public debate on this side of our border. This factor can no longer be ignored.
Later this year policy measures which emerged from the inquiry's recommendations, from provincial and public discussions and the task force will be discussed in Cabinet. At that point the position of the federal Government on water export in general, and on such proposals as the Grand Canal in particular, will be made much clearer.
To conclude, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill can rest assured that the federal Government will take no action on the Grand Canal until the national water policy is clearly established and in place. That policy will recognize the very complex and controversial nature of this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a minute or two to speak on this Private Members' Bill. I have always enjoyed Private Members' Hour because we hear different perspectives from Hon. Members who come from different regions of the country. I am always amazed at the official position of the New Democratic Party, which has truly become an entrenched ultraConservative Party. It does not even want to study any question. Rather than being opposed to studying a question, if that Party is convinced something is not good for the country, there is all the more reason to have these studies in order to verify the points they put forth so strongly. It seems to me the
Government has a positive duty to study the issue so that it can be settled.
This country has always relied upon its resources. If we had accepted the position of the New Democratic Party on development, we would have no development. Canada would never have come to exist. We started with fish. That meant fish had to be pulled out of the sea, which made for fewer fish. We then moved on to beaver. We all appreciate what the beaver meant to the early development of Quebec, northern Canada and Ontario. The buffalo had its use for leather in the West. Then there was oil and gas. This country is immensely more rich and our standard of living is higher because we used and developed our resources. It seems incongruous to me that the Socialist Party seems in favour of exporting a reasonable amount of oil and gas, which is a non-renewable resource, yet is opposed to a study with respect to exporting water, which is perpetually renewable. If I had to choose, I would far rather keep our petroleum products in the ground for our grandchildren and great grandchildren than our water, which flows off and is forever lost.
I think we ought not to forget that our life-style, which is very high indeed, depends on the use of our resources. That is not to say that we should exploit those resources and destroy our environment. We very much need to spend our time studying ways in which to use our resources so that they will be available 10 generations down the road. We have much to learn. If we do not develop our resources, we might have to be prepared to see our life-style drop by 50 per cent or 75 per cent. I do not believe people are prepared to let that happen.
I personally-and we all speak personally in Private Members' Hour-see the Grand Canal concept as an enormous opportunity, just as the Lachine Canal has enhanced our standard of living and just as the Rideau Canal provides immense enjoyment for thousands of tourists and has created thousands of jobs. We have the Welland Canal and the St. Lawrence Seaway. Just think of what the Grand Canal would mean to those 4,000 unemployed engineers in the city of Calgary alone. Those engineers should be put to use. We have spent billions of dollars in a very expensive educational system, giving our young people a high level of education for which we are not providing jobs.
It strikes me as very worth while to study this project. I would stand four-square behind the study. How are we going to get $12 billion to pay for our old age security if we do not make the investment today? If we do, our children can have the jobs which will create the wealth so that they can look after us when we are old. If there had been no CPR, I for one, as well as I suppose six million other people in the West, would not be here today. When Canada was created in 1867, there were a mere three million people in Ontario and Quebec, primarily on farms. The Government had the wisdom to buy Rupert's land from the Hudson's Bay Company. It then had the wisdom to invest more money to build the CPR so that millions of our ancestors could come in and settle that great western plain.



May 1, 1986

Coming from a semi-desert area, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I know what water can do. A piece of land worth perhaps $20 an acre can increase in value to $2,000 or $3,000 an acre with water. Those things have increased our standard of living so that we can afford old age security for our seniors and university education for our children.
In conclusion, I will say that I generally believe that we as a Government should be prepared to study anything which will put our people to work, which will develop this country so we can maintain a standard of living to which we have become accustomed, and which will provide a future for our children and grandchildren.

IMMIGRATION-UNSCRUPULOUS IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the Adjournment Debate. My question follows from a question I directed to the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean) on April 18. It concerns the whole issue of the refugee determination process with which we as a Parliament and as a Government need to come to terms. Within that framework, the Minister of State for Immigration publicly and in the House has said that he would like to rid the system of phoney refugee applications.
I think there is some degree of unanimity on that score simply because there are a great number of legitimate claims which will certainly be hampered by those which are illegitimate. The backlog is becoming serious and alarming. As you may know, Mr. Speaker, it numbers 21,000 and is rising. We need to maintain a sense of balance. If the Minister wants to rid the system of "phoney refugees", then I believe he has to come to terms with the question of phoney immigration consultants and phoney immigration lawyers. I say "phoney" advisedly. I mean those who prey on innocent individuals. They are so-called immigration lawyers who are charging exorbitant fees for services which are readily available at our immigration offices and through the normal channels here in Canada. They are individual consultants and lawyers who are using fraudulent schemes in terms of advertising in other countries about a system with respect to how people can come to Canada.
Adjournment Debate
Once these people come to Canada, they face a reality which is very different from what it was purported to be. They face deportation. Therefore, what we have is a large number of individuals who claim refugee status based on advice and advertisements which are clearly delineated by the so-called consultants. As a last resort, these people put in a claim for refugee status rather than face deportation. A good number of individuals have given up their lives in the other country. They have sold their homes and properties. They come to Canada with the expectation that what the so-called immigration consultants told them was the truth. Much to their disbelief, they find out that there is a different reality once they come to Canada.
This issue was recently brought to light as a result of the so-called problem facing the Portuguese-Canadian community. There were a large number of individuals from Portugal claiming refugee status based on the grounds of religious persecution. If we are to react, as the Minister has, in terms of a rating system for phoney refugees, then we cannot do that without addressing ourselves to the question of phoney immigration consultants and lawyers. This is why on April 18 I asked if the Minister had the intention of offering some balance into the equation. I asked whether he or his colleague, the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty), intended to prosecute those who are preying on innocent individuals. The Department has specific information about a number of such practices, specifically in Toronto, with regard to the Portuguese-Canadian community. There is inaction on the part of the Government in terms of putting a stop to those individuals who are using fraudulent schemes and who are exacerbating the problem of the refugee backlog.
Another interesting argument is the possibility that the Minister of State, as a result of the increasing number of refugee claimants based on the grounds of religious persecution in Portugal, will clamp visa requirements on Portugal. I raised a question in the House with respect to this matter on another occasion. Today, I submit that that is an incorrect, knee-jerk reaction. If we were to clamp a visa requirement on Portugal, we would be doing a disservice to a European friend and ally. We would be punishing the majority for what is a small minority-type problem. That is to say, of the 21,000 people who make up the backlog, approximately 1,000 of those are from Portugal. If we use the logic of the Minister of State and impose visa requirements on Portugal, which represents
1,000	of the 21,000 backlogged cases, then what are we to do with other countries which have the remainder of refugee claimants?
I am interested today in pursuing this discussion to see what the Minister of State is thinking with regard to the whole question involving the refugee problem and specifically as it relates to the Portuguese dilemma. On the one hand we need to come to grips with these consultants and immigration lawyers who are coming across with tactics which should not be tolerated. If we come to grips with them, then we will be

May 1, 1986
Adjournment Debate
heading in the right direction in terms of solving the problem and in terms of limiting the number of fraudulent refugee claimants from that particular country and, indeed, from other countries. In this way we would be sending out the proper signals that we will not tolerate individuals of that kind.
I am looking for assurance that the Government will not impose visa requirements on Portugal, thereby making it the only country in western Europe with visa requirements. That is not the proper way of addressing the refugee backlog. The proper way would be to bring in a comprehensive refugee determination process that is fair and equitable to everyone and does not specifically target one country with the problem. I see that my time is up, and I look forward to the Parliamentary Secretary's response.

subtopic: TRADE-THREATENED USE OF SUBSIDIES TO SELL UNITED STATES WHEAT TO SYRIA. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
TRADE-THREATENED USE OF SUBSIDIES TO SELL UNITED STATES WHEAT TO SYRIA. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, I raised in the House the question of the possible sale of wheat by the United States to the country of Syria. On April 8, Syria was offered 700,000 tonnes of American wheat.
No sales have yet been announced, but the Americans decided to use their export enhancement program of the Farm Bill to subsidize the sale of wheat to the great country of Syria.
Syria has been a traditional Canadian customer. When we sell wheat to Syria, we cannot use subsidies under the Canadian Wheat Board. The Government does not subsidize the export of Canadian wheat. My concern is that the Americans will go into Syria with great big subsidies and, since we do not have any subsidies at all, we will not be able to compete. We are going to lose many of our traditional markets in the country of Syria. That is of great concern to farmers right across western Canada and to Canadians in general because if farmers go broke, there will be a loss of jobs right across the country.
I am very concerned about growing protectionism in the United States and about the American Farm Bill that President Reagan signed into law last December, which adds even more export subsidies to American grain exporters and subsidizes to an even greater extent the American farmer.
I would like to put on record how the American export program, the BICEP program, works. In the last five months, there have been 11 separate sales to Algeria by the United States, totalling one million tonnes of U.S. grain. These sales were made at prices as low as $85 American per tonne. That sale occurred on February 28, 1986. In March, a sale was made at $88 American per tonne. On October 23, a sale of $103 American per tonne was made. We can see that their selling price runs from $85 to $103 American. At the same time, their sales are subsidized by anywhere from $23 per tonne to $54 per tonne.
The best example would be the sale which occurred on October 23, 1985. At that time the Americans sold 135,000 tonnes of grain to Algeria. The selling price was $103 per tonne and the subsidy was $54.38 per tonne. What the Americans have really said to the Algerians is that they would sell them two bushels of wheat at $103 per tonne and give them one free. How can we, as Canadians, compete against such a policy?
I know the European Common Market is not any better. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said the other day that it was a little better than the Americans, but not much. We have two big giants, two cowboys fighting it out in a trade war-the Americans and the Europeans. We as Canadians, along with the Argentinians, are caught in the middle.
It is not only Syria and Algeria. I have figures for a number of other countries. I will give a few more examples in the short period of time I have available to me. The Americans have made four sales to Egypt, going back to September, 1985. These sales involved wheat flour, soft red winter wheat, and frozen poultry. In all cases the sales were massively subsidized. For example, in the case of frozen poultry, the Americans sold
8,000	tonnes on December 27, 1985 at $558 per tonne, and the
May 1, 1986

subsidy was $345.46 per tonne. These are official government figures which the Minister has confirmed he has in his possession.
Another example would be the sale of wheat flour by the Americans to Yemen on January 28 and on February 14, Valentine's Day. The sales involved 31,500 tonnes of wheat flour at $166 per tonne, and the subsidy was $123 per tonne. How can we compete for the market of Yemen when the United States provides such a massive subsidy?

And the other country is Morocco, Mr. Speaker. There were five sales of Canadian wheat to Morocco. The price was about the same as for Algeria: $106 per ton, with a subsidy of $20, $22, $24 and $25 per ton. Mr. Speaker, that is not fair at all.

Another example is Turkey. There were six sales to Turkey, going back to November, 1985. The selling price was from $100 to $115 per tonne, and the subsidies were between $18 and $38 American per tonne. Once again, how can we as a country compete?
Another example is the Philippines. Many sales were made and there were large subsidies. In the case of Zaire, there were sales of wheat flour and hard red winter wheat, again with massive subsidies.
Of course there are other countries where sales have not been made, but the Americans are trying to make such sales. One would be Syria, about which I raise a .question this evening. Their sale of 700,000 tonnes to Syria represents the entire Syrian wheat market for one year. Last year I think we had about 45 per cent or 46 per cent of that market, and the Americans only had about 6 per cent or 7 per cent. They are trying to use the same program of subsidies to get into the markets of Iraq, Nigeria, Tunisia, and Benin. That is only the beginning of the list. I am convinced that they will try to use the same subsidies to go into the Soviet Union, China, and perhaps South Korea, other very good traditional Canadian markets.
I want the Government to take a strong stand with the Americans and with the Europeans. It should tell them that this kind of trade war is not right and lodge a complaint with the International Wheat Council in London. It is wrong; it is a violation of the International Wheat Agreement, if not the letter of the law, certainly the spirit of the law. The Government should raise this question at GATT and in Tokyo. It should speak out on the world scene.
Let us not be timid. Let us stand up for Canada. Canada is a great country. Let us take a strong stand for Canada against what the Americans and Europeans are doing. Otherwise, our farmers will go under. They will not survive with $3 per bushel when the Americans are getting $6. Mr. Speaker, you are from the Northwest Territories and I am sure, even though there are no grain farms in your riding, you know exactly what I mean.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to respond to the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). I was afraid he would not show. However, better late than never, and I would like to respond to his comments.
Mr. Speaker, during the 1984-85 harvest year, Syria imported 1.5 million tons of wheat. Canada has 45 per cent of this market, European countries 40 per cent and the United States 9 per cent.
In the past, the United States have always given us the assurance that their export program was not aimed at Canada's traditional markets. It was aimed at subsidized markets such as those of the European Economic Community rather than markets like ours.
We have an excellent reputation as a result of the quality and consistency of Canadian wheat exports. Our fertile soil, our inspection system, an efficient transportation network and recognized trading practices are all factors that have helped to build and strengthen this enviable reputation.
It is thanks to this reputation that we keep our customers. The selling price is one of many arguments that may tip the scales one way or another.
Mr. Speaker, the real problem is not the projected sale of American wheat to Syria, but an escalating subsidy war between the EEC and the United States.
Our Government is reacting on several fronts, Mr. Speaker, both on the international market and in our own country.
The Prime Minister is now on his way to the Tokyo Summit, where Canada has put agricultural trade at the top of its priority list. This step shows how serious this Government is about maintaining our export markets.
Earlier today, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) met with agricultural organization leaders before taking off for Tokyo. He wanted to know their views before discussing, with the summit participants, the escalating war of grants between the EEC and the United States.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers just happen to be in the line of fire, and it was precisely to help them that yesterday the Prime Minister unveiled a series of very important measures. This Government has always been a strong supporter of the agricultural community, and yesterday we made another significant contribution. The Government has decided to raise domestic wheat prices, which will now range from $6 to $11 a bushel. A special committee of the House of Commons has just launched a series of hearings on the pricing of domestic wheat. In addition, the Government has decided to freeze the farmers' share of wheat transportation costs during the 1986-87 crop year. This represents savings of $40 million for our wheat growers.

May 1, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is running out, but I would have a lot more to say about this very important question. We have removed all federal excise and sales taxes on diesel and gas used on farms. The federal tax rebate now given to producers for fuel sold to farmers will be increased to 5.5 cents a litre, a measure which entails net savings of $165 million over the next two years. The total 5.5-cents-a-litre rebate will rise to 6.5 cents on January 1, 1987.

subtopic: TRADE-THREATENED USE OF SUBSIDIES TO SELL UNITED STATES WHEAT TO SYRIA. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
